narrative:
The model predicted a 74.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These consistently low academic rankings in law school were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Working part-time was the third most important factor and also nudged the outcome toward failure. Only 7% of accepted students planned to work part-time, while the vast majority (93%) attended full-time. Your choice to work while studying signaled to the model that you would have less time to prepare thoroughly for the exam.

Your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.7, both noticeably below the averages of accepted students (37 and 3.23), added to the concern but carried less weight than your law-school performance and study intensity.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class ranking through intensive study, consider switching to full-time enrollment if possible, and retake the bar-prep courses. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to this rejection. (248 words)
